chunks: "A shield works by two mechanisms: reflection and absorption.
When a wave hits a metal surface, the wave impedance, 377 ohms in the far field, is far higher than the metal's surface impedance, milliohms, so almost all of it reflects.
The small fraction that enters is absorbed: the field induces eddy currents in the metal that oppose it, so it decays exponentially with a skin depth.
For copper at 100 megahertz the skin depth is 6. 6 microns, so a 35 micron foil is more than five skin depths and gives about 46 decibels of absorption on its own.
In the near field the picture changes.
An electric field source is high impedance, so reflection is very high, and you can shield it with any grounded conductor: it's just electrostatic shielding, the field lines terminate on the shield.

A magnetic field source like an inductor is low impedance, so reflection is poor, and at low frequencies a thin non-magnetic shield absorbs little; for 100 kilohertz, copper foil is hardly better than nothing, so you either use thick or high-permeability material like steel or mu-metal, or reduce the loop and increase distance.
And whatever the metal does in theory, the real shielding is set by leakage: seams, vents and unfiltered cables. A 10 mm slot only gives about 16 decibels at 2. 4 gigahertz."
